'''Whitman''': {{legend0|#ffb2b2|40–50%}} {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} | title = U.S. Senator | before_election = [[Bill Bradley]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[Bill Bradley]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{Elections in New Jersey}} The '''1990 New Jersey United States Senate election''' was held on November 6, 1990. [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] incumbent [[Bill Bradley]] was narrowly re-elected to a third term in office over little-known Republican [[Christine Todd Whitman]].{{cite web |url=http://clerk.house.gov/member_info/electionInfo/1990election.pdf |title=Statistics of the Congressional Election of November 6, 1990 | last=Dendy |first=Dallas L. |format=PDF}} Whitman came surprisingly close to defeating the popular Bradley, and her overperformance in this election set her up to run for [[governor of New Jersey]] [[1993 New Jersey gubernatorial election|in 1993]]. ==Democratic primary== ===Candidates=== * [[Bill Bradley]], incumbent U.S. senator since 1979 *Daniel Z. Seyler, [[Phillipsburg, New Jersey|Phillipsburg]] resident ===Results=== {{Election box begin no change | title = 1990 Democratic U.S. Senate primary{{cite web |title=United States Senate - Primary Election, June 5, 1990 |url=https://nj.gov/state/elections/assets/pdf/election-results/1990/1990-primary-election-results-us-senate.pdf |website=New Jersey Division of Elections}}}} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | party = Democratic Party (United States) | candidate = [[Bill Bradley]] (incumbent) | votes = 197,454 | percentage = 92.38% }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change | party = Democratic Party (United States) | candidate = Daniel Z. Seyler | votes = 16,287 | percentage = 7.62% }} {{Election box total no change | votes = 213,741 | percentage = 100.00% }} {{Election box end}} ==Republican primary== ===Candidates=== *[[Christine Todd Whitman]], president of the [[New Jersey Board of Public Utilities]] and former [[Somerset County, New Jersey|Somerset County]] [[Board of county commissioners (New Jersey)|freeholder]] (1983–88) ====Declined==== *[[Leanna Brown]], state senator from [[Chatham, New Jersey|Chatham]]{{cite news|title=Brown decides against a run for U.S. Senate|date=24 Feb 1990|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/253790178|url-access=subscription|access-date=14 Oct 2022|newspaper=[[The Record (New Jersey)|Daily Record]]|last=O'Dea|first=Colleen|page=3}} ===Campaign=== The New Jersey Republican Party struggled to recruit a candidate to oppose Bradley, a widely popular incumbent with financial resources in a state that had not elected a Republican to the Senate [[1972 United States Senate election in New Jersey|since 1972]],{{cite news|title=GOP'S Whitman to Face Sen. Bradley|last=Hester|first=Tom|date=13 Mar 1990|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/318009540/|url-access=subscription|access-date=14 Oct 2022|newspaper=[[Central Jersey Home News]]|page=3}} although incumbent Republican President [[George H. W. Bush]] had [[1988 United States presidential election in New Jersey|carried the state by a wide margin in 1988]] and remained highly popular. The two most commonly mentioned candidates were [[Christine Todd Whitman]], the president of the state board of public utilities, and State Senator [[Leanna Brown]], who had raised her profile through her involvement in Jim Courter's 1989 gubernatorial campaign. Brown removed herself from consideration on February 24, leaving Whitman as the likely nominee. Bradley was expected to outspend the Republican nominee four-to-one and even Whitman admitted that the goal of the Republican campaign was not winning, but rather "show[ing] there are good credible candidates... to show there is life after [[Thomas Kean|Tom Kean]]."{{cite news|title=BPU's Whitman considers challenging Bradley|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/317968026/|date=25 Feb 1990|last=Serrill|first=Ted|url-access=subscription|access-date=14 Oct 2022|newspaper=[[Central Jersey Home News]]|page=13}} Whitman, the daughter of former party chair [[Webster B. Todd]], resigned from the public utilities board on March 5 and announced she would face Bradley with the support of the state party on March 13. In doing so, Whitman passed up the opportunity to run for an open U.S. House seat vacated by [[Jim Courter]]. Acknowledging the uphill battle Whitman faced, Somerset party chair [[John S. Penn|Jack Penn]] compared her odds to those of [[Buster Douglas]], a 42:1 [[underdog]] who had [[Mike Tyson vs. Buster Douglas|knocked out]] [[Mike Tyson]] one month earlier. ===Results=== {{Election box begin no change | title = 1990 Republican U.S. Senate primary}} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change | party = Republican Party (United States) | candidate = [[Christine Todd Whitman]] | votes = 112,214 | percentage = 100.00% }} {{Election box total no change | votes = 112,214 | percentage = 100.00% }} {{Election box end}} ==General election == ===Candidates=== * [[Bill Bradley]], incumbent U.S. senator since 1979 (Democratic) * John Kucek (Populist) * Don Mackle (Socialist Workers) * Louis Stefanelli (Libertarian) * [[Christine Todd Whitman]], president of the [[New Jersey Board of Public Utilities]] (Republican) ===Campaign === U.S. Senator Bill Bradley didn't realize he was in danger of losing re-election and the [[New Jersey]] voters' anger over taxes and economy until the week prior to the election. In the early part of the campaign, Bradley already had a major image problem; he was comfortably ahead in the polls, so his staffers told him to play it safe. He aired television advertisements of himself walking on the beach, shooting a perfect shot on the court, and sitting back in his office with his basketball shoes on his desk. The advertisements backfired as voters were turned off and thought that he wasn't taking his job seriously, especially at a time when voters were suffering.{{citation needed|date=October 2022}} Another major problem with Bradley was how Democratic Governor [[Jim Florio]] implemented a $2.8 billion tax increase, hurting the state's economy. In addition, Bradley refused to answer questions pertaining to Florio's tax policies.{{citation needed|date=October 2022}} After Bradley realized he was in trouble, he released negative advertisements attacking Whitman's own record on taxes, accusing her of favoring tax increases when she was a Somerset County Freeholder. Bradley's image may have been further damaged by his newer advertisements.{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1990/11/08/nyregion/1990-elections-what-went-wrong-bradley-says-he-sensed-voter-fury-but-it-was-too.html?pagewanted=1|title=THE 1990 ELECTIONS: What Went Wrong?; Bradley Says He Sensed Voter Fury but It Was Too Late to do Anything|newspaper=The New York Times|date=8 November 1990|last1=King|first1=Wayne}} ===Polling === {| class="wikitable" style="font-size:90%" |- valign=bottom !
